chunks: And Muhammad ibn Hammam informed us, saying: Ja'far ibn Muhammad ibn Malik and Abdullah ibn Ja'far al-Himyari narrated to me, saying: Muhammad ibn al-Husayn ibn Abi al-Khattab, Muhammad ibn Isa, and Abdullah ibn Aamir al-Qasabani all narrated to us, from Abdurrahman ibn Abi Najran, from al-Khashshab, from Ma'roof ibn Kharrabooth, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said: I heard him say: The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said:

"The example of my family in this umma is like the stars of the sky. Whenever a star sets, another rises. Until when you stretch your eyebrows towards it and point with your fingers at it, the Angel of Death comes to take it with him. Then you remain for a period of time, not knowing which one is which, so the sons of Abdul Muttalib become equal in that regard. While you are in that state, Allah will make your star shine again. Then praise Him and accept it."

key_terms.بَنُو عَبْدِ الْمُطَّلِبِ: The sons of Abdul Muttalib (progeny of the Prophet)

ai.seo_question: What is the metaphor used for the succession of the Imams in Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Nu'mani’s *Kitab al-Ghayba* employs the metaphor of stars to illustrate the continuity of divine guidance through the Imams, ensuring the community remains anchored even during periods of occultation. It specifically highlights the era of the Major Occultation (al-Ghayba al-Kubra) as a time of uncertainty where the identity of the Imam is veiled, culminating in the reappearance of the 'star' (al-Mahdi) to restore justice. This narrative underscores the Shia belief in the infallible lineage of the Ahl al-Bayt as the enduring source of spiritual and temporal authority.
